clinician.current_trajectory_hypothesis: The patient presented with chronic vision reduction and large eyes, suggesting a congenital or early-onset ophthalmic condition. Initial examination findings are needed to differentiate between subluxated cataract and congenital glaucoma.

report.source_text: Physical examination showed that best corrected visual acuity (BCVA) of counting finger at one and three meters in the right and left eyes respectively. Average repeated IOP measured by I- care tonometer was 12 mmHg for right eye and 11 mmHg in the left eye. Pupils were equal in size and reactive to light, there was no relative afferent pupillary defect. Horizontal corneal diameter was 14mm (Figure 1) in both eyes with stromal opacities and Haab's striae (Figure 2). Anterior chambers were deep and gonioscopy revealed wide open angles in both eyes. There was iridodonesis, phacodonesis, as well as superiorly and nasally subluxated cataract lenses in both eyes. The cataract in the right eye was denser.

Initial IOPs are normal. Optic disc findings are crucial to assess the extent of glaucomatous damage and support the 'spontaneously arrested' aspect of the diagnosis.

report.source_text: After counseling and discussion on prognosis with the patient, manual small incision cataract surgery was done for the right eye. On 2nd post-operative week, the right eye BCVA was 6/36 and poor vision was explained by amblyopia. After one month the IOP was normal, but intraocular lens (IOL) was dislocated and BCVA decreased to 6/60.

clinician.final_diagnosis: The diagnosis of subluxated cataract of both eyes, but denser on right and spontaneously arrested primary congenital glaucoma was reached.
clinician.trajectory_summary: A 32-year-old man presented with chronic vision reduction and large eyes since childhood. Initial ophthalmic examination revealed bilateral large corneal diameters (14mm) with stromal opacities and Haab's striae, suggesting past congenital glaucoma. Intraocular pressures were normal (12 mmHg OD, 11 mmHg OS) and fundoscopy showed pink optic rims with 0.6 C/D ratio and no nerve fiber layer loss, indicating spontaneously arrested glaucoma. Additionally, bilateral superiorly and nasally subluxated cataracts were found, denser in the right eye, with iridodonesis and phacodonesis. Manual small incision cataract surgery was performed on the right eye. Post-operatively, the right eye's BCVA was 6/36, attributed to amblyopia. One month later, the intraocular lens dislocated, and BCVA decreased to 6/60. No further information regarding the management of the dislocated IOL or the left eye's cataract is available.

key_supporting_evidence.claim: Patient presented with reduction of vision of 2 year duration, worsening from childhood, and large eyes since childhood.
Ophthalmic examination revealed bilateral large horizontal corneal diameter of 14mm with stromal opacities and Haab's striae.
Intraocular pressure was normal (12 mmHg OD, 11 mmHg OS).
Fundoscopic examination showed pink optic rims with vertical cup-to-disc ratio of 0.6 in both eyes with no nerve fiber layer loss.
Bilateral iridodonesis, phacodonesis, and superiorly and nasally subluxated cataract lenses were present, with the right eye's cataract being denser.
Manual small incision cataract surgery was performed on the right eye.
Post-operative course for the right eye included an initial BCVA of 6/36, followed by IOL dislocation and decreased BCVA to 6/60 after one month.
